problem: Term drift: 'manners' here is moeurs (the whole set of customs and dispositions), not etiquette; style note requires 'customs'/'mores'.
replacement: But apart from this reason, there are several others that will at all times habitually lead men to prefer equality to freedom. If a people could ever succeed in destroying the equality that prevails within it, or even in reducing it, it could do so only through long and laborious effort. Its social condition would have to be changed, its laws abolished, its opinions replaced, its habits altered, its mores corrupted. Political liberty, on the other hand, is more easily lost: to neglect to hold it fast is to let it slip away. Men therefore cling to equality not only because it is dear to them but also because they believe it will last forever.

problem: Term drift: 'manners' (moeurs) kept in the sense of etiquette; should be 'mores' or 'customs'.
replacement: What I have said applies to all democratic nations. What I am about to say concerns the French alone. Among most modern nations, and especially among all those of the Continent of Europe, the taste for freedom and the idea of it began to exist and to spread only when social conditions were tending toward equality, and as a consequence of that very equality. Absolute kings were the most effective levelers of ranks among their subjects. Among these nations equality came before freedom. Equality was therefore a long-established fact while freedom was still a novelty. Equality had already created customs, opinions, and laws of its own when freedom, alone and for the first time, came into actual existence. So freedom was still only a matter of opinion and taste, while equality had already crept into the habits of the people, taken hold of their mores, and given a particular turn to the smallest actions of their lives. Is it any wonder that the men of our own time prefer the one to the other?

problem: 'to the ruin of both' is an addition not in the source ('mutually and perniciously complete and assist each other').
replacement: Despotism is very timid by nature, and it is never more sure of lasting than when it can keep men apart. All its influence is commonly exerted for that purpose. No vice of the human heart suits it so well as egotism. A despot readily forgives his subjects for not loving him, provided they do not love one another. He does not ask them to help him govern the state. It is enough that they do not aspire to govern it themselves. He brands as turbulent and unruly those who would combine their efforts to promote the prosperity of the community, and, twisting the natural meaning of words, he praises as good citizens those who have no sympathy for anyone but themselves. Thus the vices that despotism produces are precisely those that equality fosters. These two things complete and assist each other, with pernicious results. Equality places men side by side with no common tie between them. Despotism raises barriers to keep them apart. Equality predisposes them not to think of their fellow creatures, and despotism makes general indifference a kind of public virtue.

problem: 'the State' (the nation, the state apart from society) left capitalized, inconsistent with ch46 p0 and the style note's lowercase 'state'.
replacement: It is difficult to draw a man out of his own circle and interest him in the destiny of the state, because he does not clearly understand what influence the destiny of the state can have on his own lot. But if it is proposed to run a road across the end of his estate, he will see at a glance that there is a connection between this small public affair and his greatest private affairs. And he will discover, without anyone showing it to him, the close tie that unites private interest to general interest. So, to interest citizens in the public welfare and to convince them that they constantly need one another in providing for it, far more can be done by entrusting them with the administration of minor affairs than by giving them control of important ones. A brilliant achievement may win you the favor of a people at one stroke. But to earn the love and respect of the people around you, you will need a long succession of small services and obscure good deeds, a constant habit of kindness, and an established reputation for disinterestedness. Local freedom, then, leads a great number of citizens to value the affection of their neighbors and kindred. It perpetually brings men together and forces them to help one another, in spite of the tendencies that divide them.

problem: 'establishments for education' narrowed to 'schools', which then repeats in the next sentence; 'diffuse' weakened to 'distribute'.
replacement: Here I speak only of those associations that are formed in civil life without reference to political objects. The political associations that exist in the United States are only a single feature amid the immense number of associations in that country. Americans of all ages, all conditions, and all dispositions constantly form associations. They have not only commercial and manufacturing companies, in which all take part, but associations of a thousand other kinds: religious, moral, serious, trivial, large or small, enormous or tiny. The Americans form associations to give entertainments, to found educational institutions, to build inns, to construct churches, to spread books, and to send missionaries to the antipodes. In this way they found hospitals, prisons, and schools. If the aim is to promote some truth or to encourage some feeling by the support of a great example, they form a society. Wherever you see the government in France, or a man of rank in England, at the head of some new undertaking, in the United States you will be sure to find an association. I met with several kinds of associations in America of which, I confess, I had no previous idea. I have often admired the extreme skill with which the inhabitants of the United States manage to set a common goal before the efforts of a great many men and to get them to pursue it voluntarily. I have since traveled through England, from which the Americans took some of their laws and many of their customs, and it seemed to me that the principle of association was by no means used so constantly or so skillfully there. The English often accomplish great things alone, whereas the Americans form associations for the smallest undertakings. It is clear that the English consider association a powerful means of action, but the Americans seem to regard it as the only means they have of acting.

problem: Awkward 'makes serve the execution of his designs'; 'Whereas if...' is a sentence fragment.
replacement: Thus the most democratic country on earth is the one where, in our time, men have carried to the highest perfection the art of pursuing in common the object of their common desires, and have applied this new science to the greatest number of purposes. Is this the result of chance? Or is there in reality a necessary connection between the principle of association and the principle of equality? Aristocratic communities always contain, among a multitude of people who are powerless by themselves, a small number of powerful and wealthy citizens, each of whom can carry out great undertakings single-handed. In aristocratic societies men do not need to combine in order to act, because they are strongly held together. Every wealthy and powerful citizen is the head of a permanent and compulsory association, made up of all those who depend on him or whom he makes serve his designs. Among democratic nations, on the contrary, all citizens are independent and feeble. They can do hardly anything by themselves, and none of them can oblige his fellow men to lend him their help. They all therefore fall into a state of incapacity if they do not learn to help each other voluntarily. If men living in democratic countries had no right and no inclination to associate for political purposes, their independence would be in great danger. But they might long preserve their wealth and their cultivation; whereas if they never acquired the habit of forming associations in ordinary life, civilization itself would be endangered. A people in which individuals lost the power to achieve great things single-handed, without gaining the means of producing them by united effort, would soon fall back into barbarism.
